notes: Hold back some liquid. A big pot loses less to evaporation per serving, so add the last of the broth at the end.
Salt and chilli: start at three-quarters of the scaled amount and taste.
Thickener scales with the liquid, not with the servings. Add it gradually.
data.tableNote: Salt is shown scaled in full. In practice, hold back a little and season at the end.

description: Scale a soup or stew up or down. The broth, vegetables, and meat scale in full, while salt, heat, and thickener need a lighter hand and a taste test.

examples.result: The scaled soup serves 12: 6 cups stock, 3 cups vegetables, 1 1/2 kg beef, 6 cloves garlic.
steps: Multiply each amount by 3: 2 cups stock become 6 cups, 1 cup vegetables becomes 3 cups.
Beef: 500 g × 3 = 1 1/2 kg. Garlic: 2 cloves × 3 = 6 cloves.
examples.title: A soup for 4, scaled to serve 12

examples.result: The halved stew serves 2: 1 cup broth, 1/2 cup carrots, 250 g beef, 1/2 teaspoon salt.
steps: Multiply each amount by 0.5: 2 cups broth become 1 cup, 1 cup carrots becomes 1/2 cup.
Beef: 500 g × 0.5 = 250 g. Salt: 1 teaspoon × 0.5 = 1/2 teaspoon.
examples.title: A stew for 4, halved to serve 2

faqs.answer: Nearly in full, but hold back a little. A big pot loses less liquid to evaporation per serving than a small one, so a tripled soup with tripled broth can end up thin. Add about three-quarters of the scaled liquid, then top up at the end if it needs it.
faqs.question: Do you scale the liquid in a soup in full?

faqs.answer: Start with about three-quarters of the scaled amount, then taste at the end. Salt and chilli concentrate as a soup simmers, and a big pot is hard to fix once it is oversalted. You can always add more.
faqs.question: How much salt goes in a scaled soup?

faqs.answer: Thickener follows the liquid, not the servings. If you held back some broth, you need less thickener too. Add it gradually, a spoonful at a time, and wait for it to thicken before adding more.
faqs.question: How do I scale the thickener in a soup?

faqs.answer: Yes. Soup is the most forgiving thing to scale, because you can taste it and adjust at the end. If it is too thick, add broth. If it is too thin, simmer it longer. If it needs salt, add salt. Very little is irreversible.
faqs.question: Can I fix a soup if the scaling goes wrong?

faqs.answer: A little longer to come to a simmer, but the cooking time after that is about the same. The vegetables and meat still need the same time to soften. Start early and check for doneness, not the clock.
faqs.question: Does a bigger pot of soup take longer to cook?

faqs.answer: Yes. Halving a soup is straightforward: halve everything, including the liquid, and use a smaller pot. The only thing to watch is the salt, which is easier to overshoot in a small pot. Start with a little less and taste.
faqs.question: Can I halve a soup recipe?

felicityNote: Soup is the most forgiving thing in the kitchen. Scale it, taste it, fix it. Nothing in a soup pot is final until you serve it.

parts.meaning: The multiplier for the bulk ingredients. From 4 to 12 servings, the factor is 3.
The number of servings you want to make. Here, 12.
The number of servings the recipe makes as written. Here, 4.
The amount of one ingredient after scaling.

formula.text: Scale factor = desired servings ÷ original servings. Scaled amount = original amount × scale factor. From 4 to 12 servings, the factor is 3.

howToSteps.name: Find the factor
howToSteps.text: Divide the servings you want by the servings the recipe makes. A soup for 4 made for 12 has a factor of 3.

howToSteps.name: Scale the bulk in full
howToSteps.text: Broth, vegetables, meat, beans, and grains all scale by the full factor. Work down the list and multiply each one.

howToSteps.name: Hold back some liquid
howToSteps.text: Add about three-quarters of the scaled broth to start. A big pot loses less to evaporation per serving, so top up at the end if it needs it.

howToSteps.name: Season at the end
howToSteps.text: Start salt and chilli at about three-quarters of the scaled amount. Taste once the soup has simmered, then add more if it needs it.

howToSteps.name: Thicken gradually
howToSteps.text: Add thickener a spoonful at a time and wait for it to work before adding more. Thickener follows the liquid, not the servings.

lede: Soup is the most forgiving thing to scale. The liquid, vegetables, and meat scale in full. Salt, chilli, and thickener do not, and the pot size sets the limit.

name: Scale a Soup or Stew
summary: Broth and veg in full, salt and heat by taste

table.caption: Scaling a soup from 4 to 12 servings: common amounts before and after

title: How to Scale a Soup or Stew Recipe
tutorial: Soup is the most forgiving thing in the kitchen to scale, and that is because you can taste it and fix it at the end. A cake is final once it is in the oven. A soup is a conversation: too thick, add broth; too thin, simmer longer; needs salt, add salt. The factor still matters, but the stakes are lower, and that makes soup the best place to learn scaling.

The bulk ingredients scale in full. Broth, stock, vegetables, meat, beans, and grains all multiply by the factor. A soup for 4 scaled to 12 uses 6 cups of stock instead of 2, 3 cups of vegetables instead of 1, and 1 1/2 kg of meat instead of 500 g. The scaler above does this one ingredient at a time, so you can work down the list and write the scaled amounts before you start chopping.

Liquid is the one thing to hold back a little. A big pot loses less liquid to evaporation per serving than a small one, because the surface area does not grow as fast as the volume. A tripled soup with tripled broth can end up thinner than the original. Add about three-quarters of the scaled liquid to start, then top up at the end if it needs it. The same logic applies to thickener: it follows the liquid, not the servings, so add it gradually and wait for it to work before adding more.

Salt and heat need the usual caution. Start with about three-quarters of the scaled salt and chilli, then taste once the soup has simmered. Flavours concentrate as a big pot reduces, and a pot of soup is hard to fix once it is oversalted. The good news is that soup is the one dish where you get to taste before you serve, so use that. Taste, adjust, taste again.

Soup is also the best batch cooking there is. A tripled pot feeds tonight and fills the freezer, and soup freezes better than almost anything else. Cool the extra portions quickly, pack them in the sizes you will reheat, and label each container with what it is and the date. A freezer with soup in it is a weeknight safety net, and it starts with a scaled up pot.
